stem: Which quotation from The Furnace at Harrow Mill most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Furnace at Harrow Mill is an 1887 novel by Ada Pellingham. Its hero, Tobias Wren, makes bottles in a factory but spends his spare hours testing new mixtures of sand, ash and lime in the hope of producing a clearer glass. Most of these trials fail. In a recent essay, one critic claims that the novel shows Wren taking real pleasure in these slow, flawed experiments, even though the factory's owners regard them only as wasted fuel:
choices: "The masters wanted bottles by the hundred, and Wren gave them bottles by the hundred, though he loathed every one."
"Each morning he fired another cloudy batch and smiled at its flaws, while the owners, passing by, muttered of squandered coal."
"He loved the moment the sand gave way to liquid, a change he thought more wonderful than any sunrise over the river."
"The owners showed his cloudy trial panes to every visitor, calling them the finest work ever made at Harrow Mill."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Wren enjoys his slow, failing experiments, and the owners think they waste fuel. In this line Wren smiles at the flaws in yet another failed batch, which covers the first part. The owners grumble about squandered coal, which covers the second. It is the only choice that shows both.

A.why: This line is about his routine factory bottles, not his experiments, and it shows him hating the work. The claim says he enjoys his experiments, so this line points the opposite way.

C.why: The line has the right tone, since Wren is clearly delighted. But it shows only half the claim: nothing here says the owners think the work wastes fuel. This is the typical trap of a line that matches the mood without matching the whole claim.

D.why: Here the owners praise the trial panes. The claim says they see the experiments as waste, so this reverses their attitude.

stem: Which quotation from Notes from a Country Surgery most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Notes from a Country Surgery (1868) is a memoir by Harriet Colvane, who practised medicine in a small farming parish at a time when vaccination against smallpox was new to many rural families. Historians of immunology often cite the book for its account of how the method spread. One historian concludes that, in Colvane's telling, villagers who at first refused vaccination were won over mainly by seeing how their own neighbours fared:
choices: "The lancet frightened them more than the pox itself, and many a door was shut against me throughout that first winter."
"By spring the smith's children, who alone had been vaccinated, were the only ones in the lane untouched by the fever."
"Mothers carried their infants to me eagerly from the first day, for they had long heard good reports of the method."
"Those who had barred their doors in autumn came to my step in April, having watched the smith's children stay well."
explanation: The claim describes a change with a cause: villagers who first refused were won over by seeing their neighbours. This line gives the refusal (the doors barred in autumn), the change (they come to her in April), and the cause (they watched the smith's children stay well). It shows every part.

A.why: This line shows only the first refusal. It never shows anyone changing their mind or the reason they did. You picked up on the fear and the shut doors, but that is only half of the claim.

B.why: This line gives the neighbours' good outcome but not the villagers' reaction to it. Nothing here shows earlier resisters being persuaded. The detail comes from the right scene but stops before the part the claim is about.

C.why: Here families accept vaccination eagerly from the start, so there is no first refusal. That goes against the claim that villagers refused at first.

stem: Which quotation from A Lantern for Old Mab most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Corwen Ashby's 1903 novel A Lantern for Old Mab follows an elderly storyteller in a remote valley who knows dozens of local tales about a cunning fox. Folklorists have praised the novel for the way it captures how oral stories actually change as they are passed on. One folklore scholar argues that Mab never tells a tale the same way twice, and that she shapes each version to suit the particular listener in front of her:
choices: "For the miller's boy the fox stayed a clever thief; for the parson's niece, the same fox learned good manners by the end."
"She never told the fox story the same way twice, and no one in the valley could say which of her tellings had come first."
"Mab held that a tale must pass from mouth to ear unaltered, just as a coin passes from one hand to the next."
"The children gathered at her hearth every evening, and even the restless miller's boy fell silent once she began."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Mab changes the tales, and she changes them to suit her listener. In this line the same fox is a thief for one child and learns manners for another. That shows the story changing, and it shows the change depends on who is listening.

B.why: This line shows that her tellings vary but gives no reason. Nothing ties the changes to the listener. It is the typical half-claim trap: you matched 'never the same way twice' and missed the second part.

C.why: In this line Mab believes tales should never be changed. That is the opposite of the claim that she changes them every time.

D.why: This line is about her audience and how well she holds their attention. It says nothing about her changing the tales. You chose it because listeners come up, but the claim is about how she reshapes the stories for them.

stem: Which quotation from "The Weaver's Account" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: "The Weaver's Account" is an 1851 poem by Elinor Tasker. Its speaker is a hand-loom weaver writing at a time when steam-powered mills were quickly taking over cloth production in her region. Textile historians often turn to the poem as a record of how craftspeople felt about this shift. One historian claims that the speaker takes pride in the quality of her own work while also grieving that machine-made cloth is replacing it:
choices: "The mill downriver hums both night and day, / And bolts of cheap bright cotton ride the cart."
"I love the clack of shuttle through the shed, / The patient rising cloth beneath my hand."
"No engine lays a thread as true as mine, / Yet I must weep to see the town in engine cloth."
"Let the mills now have the market; I am glad / To lay my shuttle down and rest at last."
explanation: The claim needs two things: pride in her own work and grief that machine cloth is replacing it. In the first line the speaker says no machine weaves as true as she does, which is her pride. In the second she weeps to see the town dressed in machine-made cloth, which is her grief. Only this choice shows both.

A.why: These lines describe the mill and its cloth, so they show the replacement. They show no feeling, though: no pride in her work and no grief. You matched the topic without matching the claim.

B.why: These lines show her love for her craft, but nothing in them mentions the machines or any sense of loss. It is the typical trap of a line with the right warm tone that covers only half the claim.

D.why: Here the speaker is glad to give up weaving to the mills. That relief contradicts the grief the claim describes.

stem: Which quotation from The Tuning of Ansel Brandt most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Margit Oller's 1912 novel The Tuning of Ansel Brandt centres on a village organist who spends his summers walking from farm to farm and writing down the songs he hears sung there. Musicologists have taken an interest in the book because it anticipates later debates about field transcription. One musicologist concludes that Oller presents Ansel as recording the songs with great faithfulness, yet privately doubting that written notation can ever truly capture them:
choices: "He wrote down every turn of the shepherd's tune, adding nothing and smoothing nothing, just as his old teacher required."
"Ansel rounded off the rough intervals so that each song would sit properly beneath the harmonies of a church organ."
"He copied each note just as the old woman sang it, then stared at the page and felt that the song had escaped him."
"In the evenings he played the collected songs for the parish, who received them with a polite and puzzled silence."
explanation: The claim pairs faithful recording with private doubt. Ansel copies each note exactly as the woman sings it, which is the faithfulness. Then he stares at the page and feels the song has escaped him, which is his doubt that notation can capture it. Both parts are in this line.

A.why: This line shows only the faithful copying. Ansel expresses no doubt about whether notation captures the song. You matched the first descriptor and stopped there, which is the half-claim trap.

B.why: Here Ansel alters the songs to fit church harmony, so he is not recording them faithfully. That goes against the first half of the claim.

D.why: This line is about how the parish reacts to hearing the songs. It says nothing about how Ansel writes them down or what he thinks of notation, so it is on topic but off claim.

stem: Which quotation from Grid and Garden most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Grid and Garden, a 1924 novel by Philip Stane, follows Lydia Marsh, an engineer hired to redesign a crowded industrial town. The book is often assigned in urban planning courses for its portrait of early zoning debates. One planning historian argues that Marsh favours straight, efficient streets only in the commercial district, and that she insists the residential quarters keep their old winding lanes:
choices: "Let the market streets run straight as rulers," she told the council, "but leave the houses their crooked lanes."
"She drew every avenue straight across the map, from the warehouses right out to the farthest row of cottages."
"Marsh loved the old town's twisting alleys, where she had wandered as a child among the bakers and the bookbinders."
"The council argued for a full week over the cost of paving the broad new streets of the commercial quarter."
explanation: The key word in the claim is 'only': Marsh wants straight streets in the commercial district and winding lanes where people live. This line calls for straight market streets and crooked residential lanes, so it matches the claim's limited scope on both sides.

B.why: In this line Marsh straightens every street, including the residential rows. That is a broader version of the claim, and it ignores the limit set by 'only in the commercial district.' You missed the scope word.

C.why: This line shows fondness for the winding lanes but says nothing about straight streets for business. It is the half-claim trap: the right mood and setting, but only one of the two parts.

D.why: This line is about the council arguing over paving costs. It doesn't show what Marsh prefers for either district, so it is on topic but doesn't illustrate the claim.

stem: Which quotation from The Tally Room most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Harlan Vosk's 1931 play The Tally Room is set in a fish cannery where workers are paid according to the total number of cans their whole line produces, not by individual output. Under this system, one slow worker lowers everyone's pay. Labour economists sometimes use the play to illustrate group incentives. One economist claims that Nell Garrity, the play's central figure, grasps this link and presses slower coworkers to keep pace because of it:
choices: "Hurry yourself along, Tom, or the whole lot of us will be stuck here long past the evening whistle again."
"The bosses count the cans at the end of the line, and they pay the whole line together, not the single girl."
"I'll work at whatever pace suits me, Tom; my wage is my own affair and nobody else's business at all."
"Pick it up, Tom. Every can you miss on this line comes out of my pay envelope as well as out of yours."
explanation: The claim has a chain: Nell understands that pay is shared across the line, and that is why she pushes coworkers. Here she tells Tom to speed up, and her reason is that every can he misses lowers her pay as well as his. The line shows both the pressure and the pay link behind it.

A.why: Nell does push Tom here, but her reason is working late, not pay. You matched the urging and missed the middle step of the chain, which is the link between pay and the group's output.

B.why: This line explains how pay is shared across the line, but Nell never presses anyone to work faster. It gives the mechanism without the action, so it is only half the claim.

C.why: Here Nell calls her wage her own affair. That denies the very link between her pay and her coworkers' output that the claim says she understands.

stem: Which quotation from The Blank Margin most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Ottilie Farrant's 1896 novel The Blank Margin, the mapmaker Jonas Pell is commissioned to chart a northern province, much of which no surveyor has yet visited. Historians of cartography have noted that the novel was written just as mapmakers were abandoning the habit of filling unknown regions with decoration. One historian argues that Pell refuses to invent features for unexplored land, even when a wealthy patron pressures him to make his maps look complete:
choices: "Pell left the whole northern quarter of the sheet empty, marked only with the plain words 'not yet surveyed.'"
"The duke wanted mountains where no one had walked; Pell handed the map back with that space still bare."
"To please the duke, Pell sketched a range of peaks and a winding river across the unknown northern hills."
"The duke admired maps crowded with sea monsters and would pay handsomely for an elaborately painted border."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Pell won't invent features, and he holds to this under pressure from a patron. In this line the duke asks for invented mountains and Pell returns the map with the space still empty. It shows both the pressure and his refusal.

A.why: This line shows Pell leaving unknown land blank, but no patron is pushing him to fill it. Without the 'even when' part, the line proves only half the claim. That is the typical trap for this question type.

C.why: Here Pell gives in and draws invented peaks and a river. That is the opposite of refusing to invent features.

D.why: This line shows the duke's taste for decorated maps, so it hints at pressure. But Pell doesn't appear, and nothing shows him refusing. You chose it for the patron and missed the claim's main point.
